rule.quote: (3) Emergency shelter care expenses, not to exceed the expenses for thirty (30) days, that are incurred for the claimant or a dependent of the claimant to avoid contact with a person who committed the violent crime.
rule.source_title: IC 5-2-6.1-21.1 (compensable losses) via Justia, 2025 Indiana Code

params.scope: replacing windows or door locks

rule.summary: Replacing windows or door locks is covered.
rule.quote: (9) Replacement of windows or door locks.
rule.source_title: IC 5-2-6.1-21.1 (compensable losses) via Justia, 2025 Indiana Code

rule.summary: Prescription drugs are covered as part of necessary medical expenses.
rule.quote: (B) prescription drugs; and (C) prosthetic devices;
rule.source_title: IC 5-2-6.1-21.1 (compensable losses) via Justia, 2025 Indiana Code

before.summary: Outpatient mental health counseling is covered, and the director may extend its 180-day expense window where justice requires, up to 2 years.

after.summary: Counseling costs must fall within 180 days of the crime, unless the director extends this where justice requires, up to 2 years.

rule.summary: Counseling costs must fall within 180 days of the crime, unless the director extends this where justice requires, up to 2 years.
rule.quote: The director may extend the one hundred eighty (180) day compensation period established by subsection (d) for outpatient mental health counseling, established by subsection (d)(7) where justice requires, but for a period not to exceed two (2) years.
rule.source_title: IC 5-2-6.1-21.1 (compensable losses) via Justia, 2025 Indiana Code

rule.summary: The program lists moving, relocation, and daily living expenses as not reimbursable.
rule.quote: Moving, relocation or daily living expenses.
rule.source_title: ICJI Victim Compensation Division (program page)

rule.summary: The program lists rent, utilities, food, travel, and lodging as not reimbursable (ambulance services are covered as medical).
rule.quote: Rent, utilities, food, travel, or lodging.
rule.source_title: ICJI Victim Compensation Division (program page)

rule.summary: Paid leave must be used first, and the program will not reimburse time covered by paid vacation, sick, or personal leave.
rule.quote: The division may not reimburse the claimant for the use of paid or otherwise compensated vacation leave, sick leave, personal leave, or other compensatory time.
rule.source_title: IC 5-2-6.1-32 (reduction of awards; collateral sources) via Justia, 2025 Indiana Code

params.extension: good cause; no application accepted more than 2 years after the crime

before.summary: The application must reach the division within 180 days of the crime; the division may extend this for good cause, but not past 2 years after the crime.

params.extension: or later if the division gives you more time for good cause. In most cases, the division cannot take an application more than 2 years after the crime

after.summary: The application must reach the division within 180 days of the crime. The division may give more time for good cause, but in most cases it cannot accept an application more than 2 years after the crime.

rule.summary: The application must reach the division within 180 days of the crime. The division may give more time for good cause, but in most cases it cannot accept an application more than 2 years after the crime.
rule.quote: the application must be received by the division not more than one hundred eighty (180) days after the date the crime was committed. The division may grant an extension of time for good cause shown by the claimant. However, and except as provided in subsections (e) and (f), the division may not accept an application that is received more than two (2) years after the date the crime was committed.
rule.source_title: IC 5-2-6.1-16 (applications for assistance) via Justia, 2025 Indiana Code

rule.summary: A claimant must have more than $100 in out-of-pocket expenses or more than $100 in lost income; this does not apply to forensic exam reimbursement.
rule.quote: (b) This section does not apply to reimbursement for forensic and evidence gathering services provided under section 39 of this chapter. (c) An award may not be made unless the claimant has incurred an out-of-pocket expense that exceeds one hundred dollars ($100) or has incurred loss of income that exceeds one hundred dollars ($100).
rule.source_title: IC 5-2-6.1-21.1 (compensable losses) via Justia, 2025 Indiana Code

before.summary: An emergency award of up to $500 may be made before the final decision if there is severe financial hardship.

after.summary: If the director finds a severe financial hardship, the director may give an emergency award of up to $500 before the final decision.

rule.summary: If the director finds a severe financial hardship, the director may give an emergency award of up to $500 before the final decision.
rule.quote: An emergency award of not more than five hundred dollars ($500) may be made by the director or his or her designee prior to the determination of final award if it is determined by the director that a severe financial hardship exists.
rule.source_title: 203 IAC 1 (Victim Services Division administrative procedure), Indiana Administrative Code

added.summary: The board may still award compensation if denying it would be a severe injustice to the victim. If more than one time limit applies, the longest one counts.

added.summary: Kansas pays only if the board finds that, without an award, the costs of the crime would cause the claimant financial stress. That means the claimant could not keep up their usual level of health, safety, and education for themselves and their dependents without undue financial hardship.
added.quote: Compensation may be awarded only if the board finds that unless the claimant is awarded compensation the claimant will suffer financial stress as the result of economic loss otherwise reparable. A claimant suffers financial stress only if the claimant cannot maintain the claimant's customary level of health, safety and education for self and dependents without undue financial hardship.

params.extension: Two years from notice of a DNA match to a suspect or of a suspect's identification; the longest applicable limit applies (74-7305(b)(3)); the board may also award if denial would be a severe injustice (74-7305(b)(2)(D)).

before.summary: Most claims must be filed within five years of the injury. If a survivor is told that DNA testing of a sexual assault kit or other evidence matched a suspect, or that a suspect was identified, they have two years from that notice. The longest deadline that applies is the one that counts, and the board can also accept a late claim if denying it would be a severe injustice.

params.extension: or within 2 years of being told a suspect was identified, through DNA or otherwise

after.summary: Most claims must be filed within five years of the injury. If a survivor is told that DNA testing of a sexual assault kit or other evidence matched a suspect, or that a suspect was identified, they have two years from that notice.

rule.summary: Most claims must be filed within five years of the injury. If a survivor is told that DNA testing of a sexual assault kit or other evidence matched a suspect, or that a suspect was identified, they have two years from that notice.
rule.quote: (A) The claim has been filed with the division within five years after the injury or death upon which the claim is based; (B) in a case where a victim who is notified that DNA testing of a sexual assault kit or other evidence has revealed a DNA profile of a suspected offender who victimized the victim or the victim on whose behalf the claim is made, or is notified of the identification of a suspected offender who victimized the victim or the victim on whose behalf the claim is made, the claim has been filed with the division within two years of such notification

before.summary: If the survivor of a sexually violent crime was under 18 when it happened, the claim can be filed up to 10 years after they turn 18.

after.summary: If the survivor of a sexually violent crime was under 18 when it happened, the board may accept a claim filed up to 10 years after they turn 18.

rule.summary: If the survivor of a sexually violent crime was under 18 when it happened, the board may accept a claim filed up to 10 years after they turn 18.
rule.quote: the victim was less than 18 years of age at the time such crime was committed, and the claim has been filed within 10 years after the date the victim turns 18 years of age

params.extension: If more than one limit applies, the longest one applies (74-7305(b)(3)).

before.summary: When the victim was under 16 and the crime was a sexually violent crime or certain trafficking or enticement crimes, the claim is due within two years of the report to law enforcement, unless a longer limit also applies.

after.summary: If the victim was under 16, a claim is due within 2 years of the report to police. This applies to a sexually violent crime and to some trafficking or enticement crimes.

rule.summary: If the victim was under 16, a claim is due within 2 years of the report to police. This applies to a sexually violent crime and to some trafficking or enticement crimes.
rule.quote: Compensation may not be awarded unless an application has been filed with the division within two years of the reporting of the incident to law enforcement officials if the victim was less than 16 years of age

rule.summary: To qualify, the crime must be reported to law enforcement within 72 hours, OR the survivor must have had a forensic medical exam within seven days, OR the board must find good cause for missing both.
rule.quote: Compensation may not be awarded unless: (1) The criminally injurious conduct resulting in injury or death was reported to a law enforcement officer within 72 hours after the occurrence of the criminally injurious conduct; (2) the victim obtained a forensic medical examination within seven days after the occurrence of the criminally injurious conduct; or (3) the board finds there was good cause for the failure to report or obtain an examination within the time limits provided in this subsection.

added.summary: Kentucky's Safe at Home Program, in the Secretary of State's office, is meant to protect victims of sexual assault, rape, other sexual crimes, domestic violence, human trafficking, and stalking. It lets victims, their minor children, and everyone who lives with them use a designated address. It is open to victims who are U.S. citizens and Kentucky residents, at no cost to them.
added.quote: The Safe at Home Program is hereby established within the Office of the Secretary of State. The Safe at Home Program shall be operated with the intent to protect victims of: (a) Domestic violence; (b) Human trafficking; (c) Stalking; (d) Sexual assault; (e) Rape; and (f) Other sexual crimes as defined by KRS 17.500. The Safe at Home Program shall authorize the use of designated addresses for victims, their minor children, and all other individuals residing with the victim. The Safe at Home Program shall be open to victims of a specified offense who are United States citizens and residents of Kentucky, without any cost to the program participant.
added.source_title: KRS 14.302 (Safe at Home Program established, designated addresses)

added.summary: The board's rule sets a $15,000 limit, except for a victim the crime leaves totally and permanently disabled. For that victim, the board may award up to $25,000, depending on funds, its rule limits, and other payment sources.

rule.source_title: Acts 2026, No. 684 (HB 969), enrolled act amending La. R.S. 46:1801 et seq.

before.summary: The board can make an emergency award of up to $1,000 while an application is pending, if a final award is likely and the claimant would face undue hardship; it is deducted from the final award.

after.summary: While an application is pending, the board can make an emergency award of up to $1,000 if a final award is likely and the claimant would face undue hardship without quick help. The emergency award is taken out of the final award. The claimant must pay back any amount above the final award, or all of it if no final award is made.

rule.summary: While an application is pending, the board can make an emergency award of up to $1,000 if a final award is likely and the claimant would face undue hardship without quick help. The emergency award is taken out of the final award. The claimant must pay back any amount above the final award, or all of it if no final award is made.
rule.quote: An emergency award shall not exceed one thousand dollars.
rule.pinpoint: La. R.S. 46:1813(B), as amended by Acts 2026, No. 684
rule.source_title: Acts 2026, No. 684 (HB 969), enrolled act amending La. R.S. 46:1801 et seq.

params.extension: the board may accept a longer period it finds justified by the circumstances

before.summary: Applications must be filed within three years of the date of the crime; this replaced the earlier one-year limit. The board can allow more time when the circumstances justify it.

after.pinpoint: Resume Digest of Act 684 (HB 969) on La. R.S. 46:1806(A)(1)
after.summary: This law changed the time to apply from one year to three years, counted from the date of the crime.

rule.summary: This law changed the time to apply from one year to three years, counted from the date of the crime.
rule.quote: Changes the time period for filing from one year to three years and provides this period begins from the date the crime is committed.
rule.pinpoint: Resume Digest of Act 684 (HB 969) on La. R.S. 46:1806(A)(1)
rule.source_title: Resume Digest, Act 684 (HB 969), 2026 Regular Session

rule.summary: An application needs reasonable documentation of the crime, which can be a law enforcement report, court records, an attestation from a healthcare provider who examined the injury, or an attestation from the provider or coroner who did a forensic medical exam.
rule.quote: (a) A report from law enforcement, rather than a police report. (b) Court records pertaining to the crime, rather than evidencing the criminal prosecution. (c) An attestation from a healthcare provider who conducted an examination of the personal injury suffered by the victim. (d) An attestation from a healthcare provider or coroner who conducted a forensic medical examination on the victim.
rule.pinpoint: Resume Digest of Act 684 on La. R.S. 46:1806(A)(2)
rule.source_title: Resume Digest, Act 684 (HB 969), 2026 Regular Session

rule.summary: Mental health counseling related to the crime is an eligible expense.
rule.quote: Approved claims may be awarded compensation for the following only if they are related to the crime (Some expenses are limited): Reasonable medical and prescription expenses Dental expenses Mental health counseling
rule.pinpoint: LCLE CVC program page, What Expenses are Eligible
rule.source_title: LCLE Crime Victims' Compensation Fund program page

rule.summary: Lost wages are paid at 80 percent of the victim's gross weekly wage, or 80 percent of the average weekly wage for seasonal or part-time work.
rule.quote: 80 percent of the gross weekly wage of the victim. For seasonal or part time wages, the amount shall be calculated at 80 percent of the average weekly wage;
rule.source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

before.summary: Relocation reimbursement is limited to $5,000 per household of the claimant.

after.summary: Moving costs are paid only when the claimant must move because of the crime for reasons of imminent danger, personal safety, or a threat of injury, up to $5,000 per household. The board rule says a police or incident report should be sent with the claim to show why the move was needed.

rule.summary: Moving costs are paid only when the claimant must move because of the crime for reasons of imminent danger, personal safety, or a threat of injury, up to $5,000 per household. The board rule says a police or incident report should be sent with the claim to show why the move was needed.
rule.quote: Reimbursement for relocation expenses is limited up to $5,000 per household of the claimant.
rule.source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

params.scope: temporary lodging or a move when moving right away is needed for the health and safety of the victim or a household member

rule.summary: Under the amended statute, temporary lodging or permanent relocation is a covered loss when moving right away is needed for the safety of the victim or a household member.
rule.quote: Temporary lodging or permanent relocation when immediate relocation is necessary for the health and safety of the victim or the victim's household member.
rule.pinpoint: Resume Digest of Act 684 on La. R.S. 46:1802 (pecuniary loss)
rule.source_title: Resume Digest, Act 684 (HB 969), 2026 Regular Session

params.scope: trips to medical care that is not available nearby, when the doctor certifies it

rule.summary: Travel beyond the first ambulance ride is paid only when needed medical care is not available locally and the treating physician certifies that; private mileage is paid at the state travel rate.
rule.quote: Transportation costs other than the initial ambulance services are reimbursable only when required medical care is not locally available. Certification is required by the physician of record that local medical care is unavailable. Allowable private vehicle mileage for out-of-town travel is reimbursed at the rate published in the current state travel regulations.
rule.source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

params.scope: replacing clothing, bedding, or other property taken as evidence or ruined by the investigation or lab tests

rule.summary: Reasonable replacement of clothing, bedding, or property taken as evidence or ruined by the investigation or lab testing is covered.
rule.quote: Expenses associated with the collection and securing of crime scene evidence are limited to: a. reasonable replacement costs for clothing; b. bedding; or c. property seized as evidence or rendered unusable as a result of a criminal investigation or lab test.
rule.source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

added.summary: Massachusetts hospitals can bill the state's victim compensation division directly for emergency room costs. This applies when the assault happened in Massachusetts and the forensic exam is done at a Massachusetts hospital.
added.quote: As of March 2016, MA hospitals are allowed to directly bill the VCAD for all Emergency Department (ED) expenses incurred as the result of a sexual assault that involve a patient whose assault occurs in Massachusetts and who receives a forensic sexual assault examination at a Massachusetts hospital.
added.pinpoint: MA SANE Protocol, Section X (Victim compensation)
added.source_title: Mass.gov DPH, MA SANE Protocol Section X: Victim Compensation

added.summary: If the victim was a minor and a criminal complaint or indictment came after the victim turned 18, the time to file starts on the date it was issued.
added.quote: If the victim was a minor when the crime was committed and the crime results in the issuance of a criminal complaint or indictment after the victim's 18th birthday, the filing period shall not commence until the date of issuance of the criminal complaint or indictment provided, however, that this exception shall not apply to claims based on the death of a minor victim.
added.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

added.summary: To get compensation, the claimant must cooperate with law enforcement in the investigation and prosecution of the crime. This does not apply if the claimant shows a reasonable excuse for not cooperating.
added.quote: A claimant shall be eligible for compensation only if such claimant cooperates with law enforcement authorities in the investigation and prosecution of the crime in which the victim was injured or killed unless the claimant demonstrates that he possesses or possessed a reasonable excuse for failing to cooperate.
added.source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 2, Eligibility for compensation

added.summary: The program may accept the physical or psychological effects of the crime as a reasonable excuse for not cooperating. A reasonable fear for the safety of the claimant or others can count too.
added.quote: The Agency may find that the physical or psychological impact of the crime and/or a reasonable fear of safety for themselves or others shall constitute a reasonable excuse and shall not constitute lack of cooperation.
added.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

added.summary: The signed application can be mailed to the MOVA office in Boston.
added.quote:
Return signed and completed application via mail, fax, or email to:

Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance
One Ashburton Place, Suite 1310
Boston, MA 02108
added.pinpoint: MOVA Application for Victim Compensation (2026, English), page 4, after section 9 (Acknowledgement)
added.source_title: MOVA Application for Victim Compensation (English)

added.quote:

added.quote:

added.source_title: MOVA Application for Victim Compensation (English)

added.summary: Attach copies of receipts for the expenses being claimed.
added.quote: Please check types of expenses for which you seek compensation and attach copies of bills and/or receipts.
added.pinpoint: MOVA Application for Victim Compensation (2026, English), page 3, section 5 (Expenses)
added.source_title: MOVA Application for Victim Compensation (English)

added.summary: The claim must come with copies of bills and other documents that verify it.
added.quote: The claim must be accompanied by copies of bills and other supporting documentation necessary to verify the claim
added.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

added.summary: A survivor who declined the forensic exam kit, or was past the kit window, must send a copy of the police report with the application.
added.quote: In these circumstances, patients must submit a copy of their police report with their Victim Compensation Application.
added.pinpoint: MA SANE Protocol, Section X (Patient declines MSAECK or patient ineligible for MSAECK)
added.source_title: Mass.gov DPH, MA SANE Protocol Section X: Victim Compensation

added.summary: For lost wages, MOVA can ask for the employer's verification of employment, dates missed, net weekly pay and leave used.
added.quote:
verification from the victim's employer (or, if self-employed, from the victim's own
records) that the victim was employed at the time of the crime
added.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

added.summary: For lost wages, MOVA can ask for a letter from a treating provider saying the victim cannot work, or can work only part time, because of the crime.
added.quote:
Upon request by the Agency, the victim must submit a disability letter from a treating health
care provider demonstrating that the victim is disabled from working full time, or limited to
working part time, as a direct result of the crime
added.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

added.summary: MOVA says a decision generally comes 4 to 6 months after applying.
added.quote: In general, you will receive a decision 4 to 6 months later.
added.pinpoint: Mass.gov, Applying for Victims of Violent Crime Assistance, 'To apply'
added.source_title: Mass.gov, Applying for Victims of Violent Crime Assistance (MOVA)

added.summary: The Address Confidentiality Program, run by the Secretary of the Commonwealth, protects survivors of sexual assault, rape, domestic violence and stalking who move to get away from the person who hurt them. It is a mail-forwarding service that gives them a protected address to use with state and local agencies, so their new address is harder to find.
added.quote: The Address Confidentiality Program (ACP) protects survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, rape, and stalking as well as some legally protected healthcare providers. Survivors often move to get away from perpetrators of violence. The Address Confidentiality Program makes their new address harder to find. The ACP is a mail forwarding service that gives you a protected address to use with state and municipal agencies.
added.pinpoint: Secretary of the Commonwealth, Address Confidentiality Program page, introduction
added.source_title: Address Confidentiality Program (Secretary of the Commonwealth program page)

added.summary: MOVA's regulation says all information it receives or keeps about a compensation claim is confidential and privileged, and anyone who gets those records from the agency may not disclose them.
added.quote: All information received, obtained or maintained by the Agency in connection with any claim for crime victim compensation shall be confidential and privileged.
added.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

rule.summary: Hospitals may not bill sexual assault exam patients for co-payments or other costs tied to their own health insurance; those amounts go to the state victim compensation program instead.
rule.quote: Hospitals may not bill patients for any co-payments or other patient-incurred costs related to their primary health insurance and those should be submitted to the VCAD.
rule.pinpoint: MA SANE Protocol, Section X (Victim compensation)
rule.source_title: Mass.gov DPH, MA SANE Protocol Section X: Victim Compensation

before.summary: The patient's own health insurance is used for the exam only if the patient opts in; otherwise the hospital bills the victim compensation program directly.

after.summary: The protocol says a patient's own health insurance can be used for the exam if the patient opts in, and that hospitals should bill the victim compensation program directly for patients who have privacy or other concerns about billing their insurance.

rule.summary: The protocol says a patient's own health insurance can be used for the exam if the patient opts in, and that hospitals should bill the victim compensation program directly for patients who have privacy or other concerns about billing their insurance.
rule.quote: While a patient’s primary health care can be used if the patient affirmatively opts in, direct billing to VCAD should be implemented for patients who have privacy/confidentiality or other concerns about their primary health insurance being billed.
rule.pinpoint: MA SANE Protocol, Section X (Victim compensation)
rule.source_title: Mass.gov DPH, MA SANE Protocol Section X: Victim Compensation

rule.summary: State guidance says a survivor who receives a forensic exam should not get a bill, including a co-pay, for the exam or the related hospital visit.
rule.quote: In Massachusetts, survivors of sexual violence who receive a forensic exam should not receive a bill (including co-pay) for the exam and/or hospital visit related to the assault.
rule.pinpoint: MSAECK survivor brochure, Payment of Related Expenses
rule.source_title: Information on the Massachusetts Sexual Assault Evidence Collection Kit (survivor brochure)

rule.summary: Covered emergency department exam expenses, including co-payments, co-insurance and deductibles, should never be billed to the survivor.
rule.quote: The expenses outlined below, including the applicable co-payment, co-insurance, and/or deductible, should never be billed to the survivor.
rule.pinpoint: Coverage and Billing Procedures for Sexual Assault Exams in Massachusetts (2018), If a Sexual Assault Forensic Exam is Administered
rule.source_title: Coverage and Billing Procedures for Sexual Assault Exams in Massachusetts (MHA/AGO/EOHHS/EOPSS guidance, approved December 2018)

params.payer: Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance (victim compensation program)
Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance (victim compensation program)

rule.summary: Exam payments do not count toward the survivor's maximum award for other crime-related expenses.
rule.quote: To ensure compliance with 28 CFR § 90.13 requiring states to provide forensic sexual assault examinations without cost to the victim, compensation paid in this section will not be considered toward the maximum award for victim's other related claims.
rule.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

params.exception: or $50,000 for a catastrophic injury

rule.summary: The maximum award is $25,000 per claimant, or $50,000 for a catastrophic injury.
rule.quote: The maximum award for compensation to a claimant pursuant to this chapter shall be $25,000; provided, however, that the maximum award for compensation to a claimant with a catastrophic injury pursuant to this chapter shall be $50,000.
rule.source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

rule.summary: Clothing and bedding seized as evidence or ruined by the investigation can be replaced up to $250.
rule.quote: A victim shall be eligible for compensation for the reasonable replacement costs of clothing and bedding seized as evidence or rendered unusable as the result of a criminal investigation that is the direct result of a crime; provided, however, that the maximum compensable amount shall not exceed $250.
rule.source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

rule.summary: A victim who was employed, or had a real job offer, can be compensated for lost earnings while medically disabled from work because of the crime, based on net earnings.
rule.quote: If the victim was employed or had received a bona fide employment offer at the time of the crime, the victim shall be eligible for compensation for loss of actual earnings due to disability from work as the result of injuries caused by the crime.
rule.source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

params.scope: rides to medical care by ambulance, chair car, dial-a-ride, taxi, or rideshare

rule.summary: Transportation to medical care is covered only for ambulance, chair car, dial-a-ride, taxi or rideshare costs.
rule.quote: Compensation for transportation costs incurred while obtaining medical care is limited to costs incurred for emergency and non-emergency ambulance service, chair car service, dial-a-ride, taxi, or ridesharing service obtained.
rule.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

rule.summary: Bus or train fares, and mileage or parking for a personal car, are not reimbursed for trips to medical or mental health care.
rule.quote: It does not include compensation for public transportation, or mileage or parking when private transportation is used.
rule.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

rule.summary: Counseling compensation may be denied for missed or cancelled appointments and for non-therapeutic court or investigative work by the provider.
rule.quote: Compensation for mental health counseling may be denied for expenses incurred in the following instances: 1. missed or cancelled appointments; 2. non-therapeutic testimonial court appearances by a health care provider; 3. non-therapeutic investigatory consultations; 4. photocopying and report writing;
rule.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

rule.summary: If the victim was a minor, the three-year filing period does not start until the victim turns 18.
rule.quote: The three-year filing period shall not commence until the victim reaches the age of 18.
rule.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

before.summary: If the claimant did not discover the crime until more than three years after it happened, the period starts at discovery, but only if there was a criminal complaint, indictment or other probable cause finding.

after.summary: If you did not discover the crime until more than 3 years after it happened, the 3 years start when you discovered it, or should have. This applies only if there was a criminal complaint, an indictment, or another finding of probable cause.

rule.summary: If you did not discover the crime until more than 3 years after it happened, the 3 years start when you discovered it, or should have. This applies only if there was a criminal complaint, an indictment, or another finding of probable cause.
rule.quote: If the claimant did not discover the act which constitutes a crime until more than three years after the crime was committed, the filing period shall not commence until the claimant discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the act which constitutes a crime; provided, however, that in such cases, the crime for which the claimant seeks compensation must have resulted in the issuance of a criminal complaint or indictment, or any other judicial or administrative determination of probable cause that an act constituting a crime has occurred.
rule.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

params.exception: or later if the program finds good cause or you were under 18

rule.summary: The crime must be reported within five days unless the agency finds good cause for the delay. Victims under 18 are not held to the five-day limit.
rule.quote: Except in the case where the agency finds such report to have been delayed for good cause, such report shall have been made within five days after the occurrence of such crime; provided, however, that a claimant who was a victim under 18 years of age shall not be required to file such report within 5 days.
rule.source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 2, Eligibility for compensation

rule.summary: A Provider Sexual Crime Report filed by a medical provider counts as a report to law enforcement.
rule.quote: Reports to local law enforcement, via a Provider Sexual Crime Report (PSCR), in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112, § 12A½, shall constitute a report to law enforcement authorities.
rule.source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

rule.summary: An award may be reduced or denied to the extent the victim's conduct provoked or contributed to the injuries.
rule.quote: To the extent that the victim's acts or conduct provoked or contributed to the injuries, the agency may reduce or deny an award to the claimant or claimants in accordance with regulations enacted pursuant to section four.
rule.source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 2, Eligibility for compensation

params.payer: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy, Sexual Assault Reimbursement Unit
Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy, Sexual Assault Reimbursement Unit
params.condition: if done within 15 days of the assault

rule.summary: The free-exam rule covers a forensic exam done within 15 days of the assault (or longer if regulation allows) and emergency hospital treatment plus follow-up testing for up to 90 days after the exam.
rule.quote: a physical and sexual assault forensic examination to gather information and evidence as to an alleged crime when the examination is conducted within 15 days of the alleged crime or a longer period as provided by regulation; (2) emergency hospital treatment and follow-up medical testing for up to 90 days after the initial physical examination
rule.source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-1007 (sexual assault exam payment)

rule.summary: A provider may not bill the survivor, the survivor's family, or the survivor's private insurance for any difference between its charges and the state's payment, and must take the state's payment as payment in full.
rule.quote: May not bill a victim of an alleged rape, sexual offense, or child sexual abuse, or the victim's family or private insurance, for any difference between charges and Department reimbursement; and (3) Shall accept the Department's reimbursement as payment in full.
rule.source_title: COMAR 10.12.02 Rape and Sexual Offenses: Physician and Hospital Charges (within COMAR 10.12 full text)

before.summary: Total compensation is capped at $45,000, including later and supplemental awards. A victim with permanent total disability can get an additional disability award on top of this total.

after.summary: Total compensation is capped at $45,000, including later and supplemental awards.

before.summary: A claim must be filed within 4 years after the crime is discovered (or a later trigger tied to an attempt to reverse a conviction).

after.summary: A claim must be filed within 4 years after the crime is discovered, or later in some cases.

rule.summary: A claim must be filed within 4 years after the crime is discovered, or later in some cases.
rule.quote: a claimant shall file a claim within 4 years after the later of: (i) the discovery of the occurrence of the crime or delinquent act or the death of the victim
rule.source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-809 (filing claims)

rule.summary: The Board can accept a late claim if there was good cause for missing the deadline.
rule.quote: A claimant may file a claim at any time if the Board determines that there was good cause for failure to file a claim within the time limits
rule.source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-809 (filing claims)

before.summary: A police report is one accepted form of evidence, not the only one. The Board must also accept medical records, a sworn statement from a qualified third party, a peace or protective order, or other probative evidence.

after.summary: A police report is one kind of evidence the Board must accept. It is not the only one. The Board must also accept medical records showing an injury that fits the crime. It must accept a sworn statement from a qualified third party, and a peace order or protective order. It must also accept any other evidence it thinks helps prove what happened.

rule.summary: A police report is one kind of evidence the Board must accept. It is not the only one. The Board must also accept medical records showing an injury that fits the crime. It must accept a sworn statement from a qualified third party, and a peace order or protective order. It must also accept any other evidence it thinks helps prove what happened.
rule.quote: The Board shall accept as evidence: (1) a report produced by a law enforcement agency; (2) medical records documenting an injury consistent with the alleged crime; (3) a sworn statement from a qualified third party; (4) a peace order issued under Title 3, Subtitle 15 of the Courts Article; (5) a protective order issued under Title 4, Subtitle 5 of the Family Law Article; and (6) any other evidence the Board considers probative.
rule.source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

rule.summary: The claimant must have at least $100 in unreimbursed expenses, or have lost at least $100 in earnings or support.
rule.quote: The Board may make an award only if the claimant, as a result of the injury on which the claim is based, has: (1) incurred at least $100 in unreimbursed and unreimbursable expenses
rule.source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

rule.summary: The Board can make an emergency award before deciding the claim if an award is likely and the claimant faces undue hardship. It may not exceed $10,000 and is deducted from the final award.
rule.quote: The amount of an emergency award under this section: (1) may not exceed $10,000
rule.source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-813 (emergency awards)

rule.summary: Unless an application is clearly without merit, the Board must make emergency awards for funeral costs, crime scene cleanup, and emergency relocation.
rule.quote: the Board shall make emergency awards for: (1) funeral expenses; (2) crime scene cleanup; and (3) emergency relocation
rule.source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-813 (emergency awards)

The Victims' Compensation Program provides direct reimbursement to hospitals and other healthcare providers who perform SAFE. Learn more about the SAFE Program on the Department of Health and Human Services' SAFE Program webpage . Notice to sexual assault victims If you have had a sexual assault forensic examination (with evidence collection kit) performed, you should know the following:

added.quote: The board may waive the time requirements of subsection 1 for good cause shown and shall waive the time requirements on behalf of a child or when the claimant is a child and the crime and the claim have been properly reported to law enforcement officers and the board by an adult who becomes aware of the crime and of the compensable injury.

added.summary: The Secretary of State runs an Address Confidentiality Program that gives victims of sexual assault, domestic violence, stalking or human trafficking a designated substitute address, which state and local agencies and courts must use instead of the real one. A survivor applies with the help of a registered application assistant, usually at a victim services program.
added.quote: The Address Confidentiality Program is established to protect victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking or human trafficking; minor victims of kidnapping; and reproductive or gender-affirming health care services practitioners by authorizing the use of designated addresses for such victims and practitioners.

added.summary: Everything the Attorney General's office holds about a compensation application or award is confidential and stays confidential with the Board. added.summary: Temporary lodging is one of the relocation costs. It counts toward the same $3,800 limit per claimant as the first month of rent, a security deposit, starting utilities, and moving costs.
added.quote: An award for expenses under this subdivision may not exceed $3,800.00 per claimant. Eligible relocation expenses under this subdivision include, but are not limited to, all of the following expenses: (i) The first month of rent, a security deposit, and the costs to start utilities in the dwelling unit to which the claimant relocates. The commission may require the claimant to provide a signed rental agreement to verify these expenses. (ii) Moving expenses, including, but not limited to, costs to rent a truck, travel, and for moving services. (iii) Costs for temporary lodging for not more than 30 days.

added.summary: Michigan's Address Confidentiality Program, run by the Department of Attorney General, gives victims of sexual assault, domestic violence, stalking, and human trafficking a designated substitute address to use instead of their real one on public records, plus free mail forwarding. Applicants must be planning to move and must apply with a certified application assistant or victim advocate.
added.quote: The Program (ACP) was created to conceal the addresses of victims of stalking, domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking, and of individuals at risk of being threatened or physically harmed from being located by their perpetrators through public records. ACP provides victims with a designated (substitute) address that can be used instead of their real address.

added.summary: The record of a proceeding before the Crime Victim Services Commission is a public record. But a claimant's file and testimony before the commission are exempt from disclosure under Michigan's Freedom of Information Act.
added.quote: The record of a proceeding before the commission is a public record, except that a claimant's file and his or her testimony before the commission is exempt from disclosure under the freedom of information act
added.source_title: MCL 18.363 (record of proceeding; claimant's file exempt from FOIA; confidentiality)

rule.summary: A health care provider may not bill a sexual assault survivor for any part of a forensic exam, including insurance deductibles, co-pays, or a denied insurance claim.
rule.quote: A health care provider shall not submit a bill for any portion of the costs of a sexual assault medical forensic examination to the victim of the sexual assault, including any insurance deductible or co-pay, denial of claim by an insurer, or any other out-of-pocket expense.
rule.source_title: MCL 18.355a (sexual assault medical forensic examination)

before.summary: If billing insurance would threaten the survivor's privacy or safety, the provider can bill SAFE Response for the exam instead.

after.summary: If you believe billing your insurance would substantially interfere with your privacy or safety, the doctor or nurse can bill SAFE Response for the exam instead.

rule.summary: If you believe billing your insurance would substantially interfere with your privacy or safety, the doctor or nurse can bill SAFE Response for the exam instead.
rule.quote: If a victim believes submitting a claim to their insurance carrier would substantially interfere with his or her personal privacy or safety, the doctor or nurse can bill SAFE Response for the forensic examination.

before.summary: Counseling is limited to 35 sessions per person plus up to 20 family sessions, at $80 per hour for a therapist or counselor and $125 per hour for a psychologist or physician.

after.summary: The program's award table lists counseling limits of 35 sessions and 20 family sessions, at $80 an hour for a therapist or counselor and $125 an hour for a psychologist or physician.

rule.summary: The program's award table lists counseling limits of 35 sessions and 20 family sessions, at $80 an hour for a therapist or counselor and $125 an hour for a psychologist or physician.

rule.summary: Lost earnings are paid at the actual loss, up to $1,000 for each week.
rule.quote: An award must not exceed $1,000.00 for each week of lost earnings.

rule.summary: Relocation expenses are capped at $3,800 per claimant.
rule.quote: An award for expenses under this subdivision may not exceed $3,800.00 per claimant.
rule.source_title: MCL 18.361 (amount of award; caps; reductions)

before.summary: Temporary or permanent relocation is covered when the move protects the survivor's safety or emotional or financial well-being, and generally must happen within 1 year of the crime or of a new threat unless good cause is shown.

after.summary: Moving costs are paid only if you move to protect your physical safety or your emotional or financial well-being because of the crime. Unless you show good cause, you must move within 1 year of the crime or of a new threat or sign of danger.

rule.summary: Moving costs are paid only if you move to protect your physical safety or your emotional or financial well-being because of the crime. Unless you show good cause, you must move within 1 year of the crime or of a new threat or sign of danger.
rule.quote: An award for expenses under this subdivision may be made only if the claimant is relocating to protect the claimant's physical safety or emotional or financial well-being as a result of the crime and, unless good cause is shown, is relocating within 1 year of the date the crime occurred, or of the date the claimant is threatened by a change in circumstance or by an indicator of danger.
rule.source_title: MCL 18.361 (amount of award; caps; reductions)

rule.summary: As part of relocation, temporary lodging is covered for up to 30 days.
rule.quote: (iii) Costs for temporary lodging for not more than 30 days.
rule.source_title: MCL 18.361 (amount of award; caps; reductions)

params.scope: trips to medical care, mental health care, a victim services organization, or a victim's funeral

rule.source_title: MCL 18.361 (amount of award; caps; reductions)

params.scope: paying someone else for child care or housework you can no longer do because of the injury or while you get victim services

rule.summary: Replacement services such as child care and homemaking are covered when the survivor cannot do them because of the injury or while attending victim services.
rule.quote: (d) Replacement services for homemaking tasks, child care, and other services previously performed by an individual listed in section 4(1)(a), (b), (e), or (f), that, because of the victim's injury, or the claimant's attendance at a victim services organization to receive services related to the crime, must temporarily or permanently be performed by another person.
rule.source_title: MCL 18.361 (amount of award; caps; reductions)

params.extension: The commission may extend the deadline for good cause on the claimant's petition (MCL 18.355(3)); for criminal sexual conduct against a minor, police-records-based rules allow filing within 5 years after the crime was reported (MCL 18.355(2)(a)).

rule.summary: A claim must be filed within 5 years after the crime.
rule.quote: a claim must be filed by the claimant not later than 5 years after the occurrence of the crime upon which the claim is based

after.summary: If the commission finds the victim or claimant chose not to cooperate with law enforcement or the prosecutor, it must turn down the claim.

rule.summary: If the commission finds the victim or claimant chose not to cooperate with law enforcement or the prosecutor, it must turn down the claim.

rule.summary: Sexual assault victims are listed as eligible for crime victim compensation.
rule.quote: The following individuals may be considered a victim and qualify for crime victim compensation: A person who was physically, emotionally, psychologically, or mentally injured as the direct result of a crime. A sexual assault victim.

added.summary: While a claim is open, the claim and its supporting documents and reports are investigative data. added.quote: Claims for reimbursement and supporting documents and reports are investigative data and subject to the provisions of section 13.39 until the claim is paid, denied, withdrawn, or abandoned. Following the payment, denial, withdrawal, or abandonment of a claim, the claim and supporting documents and reports are private data on individuals as defined in section 13.02, subdivision 12 ; provided that the board may forward any reimbursement claim forms, supporting documents, and reports to local law enforcement authorities for purposes of implementing section 611A.67

rule.quote: for the examination of a victim of criminal sexual conduct that occurred in the state shall be paid by the state. rule.summary: A claim must be filed within three years of the victim's injury. rule.summary: The crime must be reported to police within 30 days. If it could not reasonably be reported in that time, it must be reported within 30 days of when it could be. A victim of criminal sexual conduct in the first, second, third, or fourth degree who reports after 30 days is treated as having been unable to report within that time.
rule.quote: the crime was not reported to the police within 30 days of its occurrence or, if it could not reasonably have been reported within that period, within 30 days of the time when a report could reasonably have been made. A victim of criminal sexual conduct in the first, second, third, or fourth degree who does not report the crime within 30 days of its occurrence is deemed to have been unable to have reported it within that period

added.summary: A state rule lists what can count as good cause for a late report or a late claim. It includes the victim's age when the crime happened and physical or mental incapacity. It also includes a delay that was reasonable given the crime and the injuries, or police or prosecutors not telling the victim about the program.
added.quote: Factors considered when determining whether "good cause" exists for extending the one-year time limit for filing a claim, or for extending the 72 hour deadline to report criminally injurious conduct to law enforcement after its occurrence include, but are not limited to the following: (a) age of the victim when the crime occurred; (b) whether the delay in filing or reporting was reasonable, considering the circumstances of the crime and the resulting injuries to the victim; (c) physical or mental incapacity; or, (d) failure of law enforcement or prosecutors to notify the victim about the crime victim compensation.

added.summary: For lost wages, an employed survivor sends a physician's letter on letterhead, an employer letter confirming the absence, and the last paystub before the crime.
added.quote: If you have an employer, you should submit a signed physician’s letter on the provider’s letterhead that details the dates and reasons you were advised to be out of work, an official employer letter on company letterhead that confirms your approved absence and your last paystub before the incident.
added.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program FAQ, 'What paperwork do I need to submit with my application?' (Lost wages)
added.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

added.summary: For lost wages, a self-employed survivor sends a physician's letter on letterhead and a signed federal tax return from the year before the crime.
added.quote: If you are self-employed or are an independent contractor, you’ll need a signed physician’s letter on the provider’s letterhead and a copy of your signed federal tax return from the year before the crime.
added.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program FAQ, 'What paperwork do I need to submit with my application?' (Lost wages)
added.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

added.summary: For dental care, a survivor may send a proposed treatment plan on the dentist's letterhead.
added.quote: You may submit a proposed treatment plan on your dentist’s letterhead.
added.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program FAQ, 'What paperwork do I need to submit with my application?' (Dental services)
added.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

added.summary: Funeral claims need a copy of the death certificate, the itemized funeral bill, and the law enforcement report.
added.quote: Submit a copy of the death certificate, itemized funeral bill and the law enforcement report.
added.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program FAQ, 'What paperwork do I need to submit with my application?' (Funeral expenses)
added.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

added.summary: The program says the average processing time is three to six months from when it receives the application.
added.quote: From the time an application is received, the average processing time is between three to six months.
added.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program FAQ, 'What happens after I submit my application?'
added.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

added.summary: North Carolina's Address Confidentiality Program, run by the Attorney General, gives relocated victims of domestic violence, sexual offense, or stalking a substitute address so assailants cannot find them through public records.
added.quote: A program in the Office of the Attorney General to protect the confidentiality of the address of a relocated victim of domestic violence, sexual offense, or stalking to prevent the victim's assailants or potential assailants from finding the victim through public records.
added.source_title: N.C. Gen. Stat. 15C-2 (Address Confidentiality Program definitions)

added.summary: To enroll, the survivor files an application with the Attorney General with help from a designated application assistant (an advocate at a victim services agency or nonprofit).
added.quote: An individual who wants to participate in the Address Confidentiality Program shall file an application with the Attorney General with the assistance of an application assistant.
added.source_title: N.C. Gen. Stat. 15C-4 (Filing and certification of applications; authorization card)

added.summary: Victims' and claimants' personal information and all information about how claims were decided (except the total amount awarded) are held confidential by the Commission and Director; medical and law enforcement records are also confidential.
added.quote: All personal information, as that term is defined in 18 U.S.C. § 2725(3), of victims and claimants and all information concerning the disposition of claims for compensation, except for the total amount awarded a victim or claimant, shall be held confidential by the Commission and Director.
added.source_title: N.C. Gen. Stat. 15B-8.1 (Privilege and records of the Commission)

rule.summary: A provider that performs a sexual assault forensic exam may not bill the survivor, the survivor's insurance, Medicaid, Medicare, or any other collateral source for it.
rule.quote: A medical facility or medical professional that performs a forensic medical examination shall not bill the victim, the victim's personal insurance, Medicaid, Medicare, or any other collateral source for the examination and other eligible expenses.
rule.source_title: N.C. Gen. Stat. 143B-1200 (Assistance Program for Victims of Rape and Sex Offenses)

rule.summary: The provider must accept the program's payment as payment in full for the exam, so no balance can be passed to the survivor.
rule.quote: A medical facility or medical professional that performs a forensic medical examination shall accept payment made under this section as payment in full of the amount owed for the cost of the examination and other eligible expenses.
rule.source_title: N.C. Gen. Stat. 143B-1200 (Assistance Program for Victims of Rape and Sex Offenses)

rule.summary: The program lists medical, counseling, dental or orthodontic, funeral, crime scene cleanup, and lost wages as accepted expenses.
rule.quote: Accepted Expenses ✓ Medical ✓ Counseling ✓ Dental or orthodontic ✓ Burial and funeral expenses ✓ Crime scene cleanup ✓ Lost wages
rule.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page, Accepted Expenses
rule.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

rule.summary: Crime scene cleanup is an accepted expense when billed by a certified biohazard cleanup company; it may include repairing or replacing doors, locks, and windows as well as cleaning blood stains.
rule.quote: Crime scene cleanup Submit the itemized bill from a certified biohazard cleanup company. Services may include repair or replacement of doors, locks and windows, as well as cleanup of blood stains.
rule.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page, FAQ: What paperwork do I need to submit? (Crime scene cleanup)
rule.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

rule.summary: Property damage or loss, lost or stolen money, and replacing property taken as evidence (for example a phone or clothing) are not accepted.
rule.quote: Not Accepted X Property damage or loss X Lost or stolen money X Replacement of property taken as evidence
rule.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page, Not Accepted
rule.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

rule.summary: Travel is listed as not accepted.
rule.quote: X Travel
rule.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page, Not Accepted
rule.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

rule.summary: Utilities and mortgage or rent are not accepted.
rule.quote: X Utilities X Mortgage or rent
rule.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page, Not Accepted
rule.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

rule.summary: Court fees and expenses are not accepted.
rule.quote: X Court fees and expenses
rule.pinpoint: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page, Not Accepted
rule.source_title: NC DPS Victim Compensation Program page and FAQ

rule.summary: Replacement services loss (paying someone for ordinary household services the injured person would have done) is limited to $200 per week for up to 26 weeks from the date of the injury.
rule.quote: Replacement service loss will be limited to a 26-week period commencing from the date of the injury, and compensation may not exceed two hundred dollars ($200.00) per week.
rule.source_title: N.C. Gen. Stat. 15B-2 (Definitions)

params.exception: or later with good cause

rule.summary: The crime must be reported to law enforcement within six months unless there was good cause for the delay.
rule.quote: The criminally injurious conduct was not reported to a law enforcement officer or agency within six months of its occurrence, and there was no good cause for the delay.
rule.source_title: N.C. Gen. Stat. 15B-11 (Grounds for denial of claim or reduction of award)

before.summary: A claim may be denied or reduced if the claimant or victim, without good cause, did not fully cooperate with law enforcement or the prosecution.

after.summary: A claim can be denied or an award cut if the claimant or victim did not fully cooperate with police or the prosecution, unless there was good cause. A claim already decided can also be looked at again for this.

rule.summary: A claim can be denied or an award cut if the claimant or victim did not fully cooperate with police or the prosecution, unless there was good cause. A claim already decided can also be looked at again for this.
rule.quote: A claim may be denied, an award of compensation may be reduced, and a claim that has already been decided may be reconsidered upon finding that the claimant or victim, without good cause, has not fully cooperated with appropriate law enforcement agencies or in the prosecution of criminal cases with regard to the criminally injurious conduct that is the basis for the award.
rule.source_title: N.C. Gen. Stat. 15B-11 (Grounds for denial of claim or reduction of award)

added.summary: Counseling is paid for no longer than 2 years from the first session.
added.quote: No longer than a two-year period beginning on the date of the first session
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: Travel is paid only when the trip is at least 150 miles round trip from home.
added.quote: Travel distance must be at least one hundred fifty miles round trip from the claimant's residence in order for the claimant to be eligible for reimbursement of travel expenses.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: The program does not pay travel costs for the victim to meet with law enforcement, or for the victim or a homicide victim's immediate family to go to court.
added.quote: The division may not pay reimbursement for travel expenses for the victim or immediate family of a homicide victim to attend court proceedings or for the victim to meet with law enforcement.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: Apply online through the ND DOCR Crime Victim's Compensation Application portal linked from the program page.
added.quote: Clicking the link below will take you to the online application for Crime Victim
added.pinpoint: Program page, Crime Victims Compensation Application and Forms
added.source_title: ND DOCR Crime Victims Compensation program page

added.summary: Allow 2 to 4 weeks for the program to process an application or a reimbursement request.
added.quote: Please allow 2-4 weeks for processing CVC application or claim reimbursement requests.
added.source_title: ND DOCR Crime Victims Compensation program page

added.summary: Submit a completed application on the program's form, signed by the claimant or a parent, guardian, or legal representative; an employer, provider, or insurer cannot apply for you.
added.quote: A claimant for benefits shall submit a completed application for compensation signed by the claimant or the claimant's parent, guardian, or legal representative on an application form prescribed by the division.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: If the crime was not reported to law enforcement in time, explain the reason for the late report in the application.
added.quote: There may be a justifiable reason for the late report. Please explain.
added.pinpoint: CVC Application Tips, Section 3 (Incident Information, continued)
added.source_title: ND DOCR CVC Application Tips (PDF)

added.summary: For medical costs, include a billing statement showing the provider's name, business address, phone number, and treatment plan.
added.quote: A request for compensation for medical services must include a billing statement containing the medical provider's name, business address, telephone number, treatment plan, and other information necessary for the division to determine the claim is for services directly related to the criminally injurious conduct.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: For dental costs, include a billing statement showing the dentist's name, business address, phone number, and treatment plan.
added.quote: A request for compensation for dental services must include a billing statement containing the dental provider's name, business address, telephone number, treatment plan, and other information necessary for the division to determine the claim is for services directly related to the criminally injurious conduct.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: For counseling, the provider's billing statement must list itemized transactions with the provider's name, business address, and phone number.
added.quote: A billing statement of itemized transactions containing the provider's name, business address, and telephone number.
added.pinpoint: CVC Mental Health Treatment Policy and Provider Verification Form (Rev. 6/2025), Verification Requirements
added.source_title: ND CVC Mental Health Treatment Policy and Provider Verification Form (Rev. 6/2025)

added.summary: For counseling, the provider returns the CVC Provider Verification Form with the billing invoice.
added.quote: The Provider Verification Form portion is to be returned with the billing invoice for reimbursement of services to the CVC program.
added.pinpoint: CVC Mental Health Treatment Policy and Provider Verification Form (Rev. 6/2025), introduction
added.source_title: ND CVC Mental Health Treatment Policy and Provider Verification Form (Rev. 6/2025)

added.summary: For lost wages, include written documentation from a medical or mental health provider and from your employer.
added.quote: A claim for reimbursement for work loss must include written documentation from a medical or mental health provider, the claimant's employer, and information the division may request that supports payment for work loss.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: For lost wages, the employer you worked for at the time of the crime completes the CVC Employer's Report.
added.quote: FORM MUST BE COMPLETED BY EMPLOYER YOU WERE WORKING FOR AT THE TIME OF THE CRIME INCIDENT.
added.source_title: ND CVC Work Loss - Employer's Report (SFN 12437, Rev. 06-2018)

added.summary: For lost wages, if you are self-employed, include a copy of your federal income tax return for the prior year.
added.quote: Self-employed victims shall provide a copy of federal income tax return for one year prior and other substantial verification of work loss or profits the division determines is necessary to support payment for work loss.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: For lost wages, a medical provider who treated your crime injuries completes the CVC Physician's Report.
added.quote: FORM MUST BE COMPLETED BY A MEDICAL PROVIDER WHO TREATED YOU FOR YOUR CRIME INJURIES.
added.source_title: ND CVC Work Loss - Physician's Report (SFN 60497, Rev. 06-2018)

added.summary: For travel and lodging, include your receipts.
added.quote: The claimant shall submit receipts for travel and lodging expenses to the division.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: For funeral and burial costs, include itemized receipts.
added.quote: The claimant shall submit itemized receipts for reimbursement under this section.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: For replacement services, include receipts showing the billed amount and the type of service.
added.quote: A claim for reimbursement for replacement services loss must include receipts for the billed amount, type of service provided, and other information necessary for the division to determine the claim is for services directly related to the criminally injurious conduct.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: For loss of support, include proof of the support the victim gave dependents before the crime, such as tax forms, a certified death certificate, or birth certificates.
added.quote: A claim for loss of support must include verification of the amount of support the victim provided to dependents prior to the criminally injurious conduct.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: Before the program pays, you or the provider must show what insurance or another collateral source paid, or that it did not cover the service.
added.quote: Before payment is made from the division, either the provider or the claimant shall provide documentation that: a. Verifies the amount paid by the collateral source; or b. Verifies the applicant or service was not covered by the collateral source.
added.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

added.summary: The program may ask you to sign its Authorization to Disclose Protected Health Information form so it can get records it needs to decide the claim.
added.quote: The DOCR may, however, require that you authorize disclosure of your health information if needed to make a determination about your claim.
added.pinpoint: Authorization to Disclose Protected Health Information, SFN 61353, Privacy Statement
added.source_title: ND CVC Authorization to Disclose Protected Health Information (SFN 61353)

added.summary: Program records about a compensation application or award are confidential and not open to the public. The law lists who may still see them.
added.quote: All other records of the division concerning the application for or award of compensation under this chapter are confidential and are not open to public disclosure.
added.source_title: N.D.C.C. ch. 54-23.4 (Crime Victims Compensation)

params.condition: if done within 120 hours of the assault

rule.summary: When an acute forensic medical exam is done for alleged criminal sexual conduct or domestic violence (within 120 hours unless good cause is shown for the delay), neither the exam nor any preliminary medical screening may be charged to the survivor, directly or through insurance or another third-party payer.
rule.quote: performed within one hundred twenty hours after the alleged crime unless good cause is shown for the delay in performing the examination. When an acute forensic medical examination is performed, the costs incurred by a health care facility or health care professional for performing the acute forensic medical examination or any preliminary medical screening examination may not be charged, either directly or through a third-party payer, to the alleged victim.
rule.source_title: N.D.C.C. ch. 12.1-34 (incl. 12.1-34-07, forensic medical examination costs)

before.summary: For a child forensic exam after alleged sexual abuse, physical abuse, or neglect, neither the exam nor any preliminary medical screening may be charged to the child or the child's parent, guardian, or custodian, directly or through insurance or another third-party payer.

after.summary: When a child's forensic exam is done, neither the exam nor any medical screening before it may be charged to the child or to a parent, guardian, or custodian. This includes billing through insurance or another third-party payer.

rule.summary: When a child's forensic exam is done, neither the exam nor any medical screening before it may be charged to the child or to a parent, guardian, or custodian. This includes billing through insurance or another third-party payer.
rule.quote: When a child forensic medical examination is performed, the costs incurred by a health care facility or health care professional for performing the child forensic medical examination or any preliminary medical screening examination may not be charged, either directly or through a third-party payer, to the alleged child victim or the child's parent, guardian, or custodian.
rule.source_title: N.D.C.C. ch. 12.1-34 (incl. 12.1-34-07, forensic medical examination costs)

before.summary: For adult victims, mental health counseling is limited to 30 sessions and $3,600 total (sessions must fall within the treatment window set by the rule).

after.summary: For adult victims, mental health counseling is limited to 30 sessions and $3,600 total.

rule.summary: For adult victims, mental health counseling is limited to 30 sessions and $3,600 total.
rule.quote: For adult victims, no more than thirty sessions, and total compensation may not exceed three thousand six hundred dollars.
rule.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

before.summary: If the provider shows a need, up to 10 more counseling sessions and up to $1,200 more may be allowed, still inside the same treatment window.

after.summary: If the provider shows a need, up to 10 more counseling sessions and up to $1,200 more may be allowed.

rule.summary: If the provider shows a need, up to 10 more counseling sessions and up to $1,200 more may be allowed.
rule.quote: If a provider substantiates the need for additional sessions, the division may allow up to ten additional sessions and up to one thousand two hundred dollars total compensation for the additional sessions.
rule.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

rule.summary: Claims for property loss or damage are not covered.
rule.quote: Claims for property loss or damage.
rule.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

params.extension: The division may extend the time for filing in the interests of justice. The admin rule lists a minor applicant, or the applicant's physical and psychological condition substantially contributing to the inability to file on time; attorney error or not knowing about the program does not count (N.D. Admin. Code 94-03-03-02(1)).
or later if the division finds the interests of justice require it

rule.summary: File within one year from the date the crime was reported to law enforcement; the program may extend this when the interests of justice require.
rule.quote: A claim for compensation must be filed within one year from the date the criminally injurious conduct was reported to a law enforcement officer. The division may extend the time for filing if it determines that the interests of justice so require.
rule.source_title: N.D.C.C. ch. 54-23.4 (Crime Victims Compensation)

before.summary: The crime must be reported to law enforcement within ninety-six hours (96 hours) unless the program finds good cause for the delay. No sexual-assault-specific alternative to a police report was found.

params.exception: or later if the program finds good cause for the delay

after.summary: The crime must be reported to law enforcement within 96 hours, unless the program finds good cause for the delay.

rule.summary: The crime must be reported to law enforcement within 96 hours, unless the program finds good cause for the delay.
rule.quote: Compensation may not be awarded unless the criminally injurious conduct resulting in injury or death was reported to a law enforcement officer within ninety-six hours after its occurrence or the division finds there was good cause for the failure to report within that time.
rule.source_title: N.D.C.C. ch. 54-23.4 (Crime Victims Compensation)

params.scope: what counts as good cause for a late report

rule.summary: Good cause for a late report includes evidence, such as medical records or verifiable third-party reports, that reporting on time would have put the applicant's health or safety at risk.
rule.quote: Evidence, including medical records or verifiable reports from third parties, which substantiate the applicant's health or safety would have been jeopardized if the criminally injurious conduct had been reported in a timely manner.
rule.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

params.scope: what counts as good cause for a late report

rule.summary: Good cause for a late report also includes law enforcement confirming that the victim feared retaliation.
rule.quote: Law enforcement substantiates there was a fear of retaliation.
rule.source_title: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 94-03-03 (application for compensation)

params.exception: or, for abuse of a child, within 3 years after the child becomes an adult

rule.summary: For child abuse or sexual molestation of a child, the report to law enforcement must be made within three years after the child reaches the age of majority.
rule.quote: In the case of child abuse or sexual molestation of a child, the criminally injurious conduct must be reported to a law enforcement officer within three years after the child reaches the age of majority.
rule.source_title: N.D.C.C. ch. 54-23.4 (Crime Victims Compensation)

before.summary: Crimes in North Dakota are covered; a North Dakota resident victimized elsewhere can apply if that place has no crime victims compensation law covering the injury.

after.summary: Crimes in North Dakota are covered. A North Dakota resident hurt by a crime somewhere else has the same rights as for a North Dakota crime if they show that place has no crime victims compensation law covering the injury.

rule.summary: Crimes in North Dakota are covered. A North Dakota resident hurt by a crime somewhere else has the same rights as for a North Dakota crime if they show that place has no crime victims compensation law covering the injury.
rule.quote: If a resident of this state is a victim of criminally injurious conduct, but the criminally injurious conduct occurred outside the geographical boundaries of this state, the resident has the same rights under this chapter as if the criminally injurious conduct occurred within this state upon a showing that the state, territory, country, or political subdivision of the country in which the criminally injurious conduct occurred does not have a crime victims compensation law which covers the bodily injury or death of the victim.
rule.source_title: N.D.C.C. ch. 54-23.4 (Crime Victims Compensation)
